subject: astronomy

moments.title: Chandrasekhar's calculation
moments.who: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, on a voyage from India to Cambridge
moments.body: Aged 19, on a ship to begin doctoral studies in Cambridge, Chandrasekhar calculates that white dwarfs cannot exist above ~1.4 solar masses; electron degeneracy pressure cannot resist gravity. The implication: more massive stellar cores must collapse further — into neutron stars or black holes. Arthur Eddington publicly mocks the result in 1935.
moments.takeaway: A 19-year-old on a boat predicted black holes. The establishment took 30 years to accept it.

now.title: Stellar remnants today
now.body: The Chandrasekhar limit (~1.44 solar masses) explains Type Ia supernovae: a white dwarf accretes mass, hits the limit, undergoes thermonuclear runaway. The standardised brightness of these explosions makes them 'standard candles' that revealed accelerating expansion (1998). Chandrasekhar received the 1983 Nobel Prize.
now.open_questions: Are there sub-Chandrasekhar Type Ia mechanisms? The picture has been complicated by recent observations.

reflection: Chandrasekhar moved from India to Cambridge to Yerkes Observatory in Wisconsin, where he commuted hundreds of miles to teach a graduate class of two students. They both won Nobel Prizes (Lee, Yang, 1957). The teacher won his in 1983.
